answers.answer: Pick the helper by its grammar role: {subject} for he/she/they, {object} for him/her/them after a verb or 'to'/'for', {possessive} before a noun, {genderedTerm} for guy/gal/person, {presentTense} for is/are, and {tense} for is/are while live and was/were when offline. For any other verb, write {verb:singular|plural} with a pipe: the first form is for he and she, the second for they. Choose the person by adding user. (the person who used the command) or target. (the person the command names). Put a capital first letter in the helper to get a capital in the reply.
answers.quote: The first form is for he and she, and the second form is for they.

answers.answer: You need to know where pronoun helpers are allowed. They work in command replies, event responses, pipelines and webhooks. The bot refuses to save them in timers and Discord notifications; only the bare {tense} works there. You also need to know which person a bare helper follows: the first word typed after the command, or the person who used the command if nothing follows. This is stated under 'Where the helpers work' and 'Pick the person'.
answers.quote: Timers and Discord notifications are not about one person, so the bot refuses to save a reply there that uses a pronoun helper.

answers.answer: Success is a reply whose words match the person's saved pronouns, as in the Examples outputs for he, she, they and any. A verb helper written without a pipe is easy to spot, because it shows in chat exactly as typed. Each helper is told apart by its role and by the person prefix (bare, user., target.).
answers.quote: Without a pipe, the bot leaves the text as you typed it, so you can see the mistake in chat.

answers.answer: When the named person has no pronouns, the bot uses the they/them words: they, them, their, person, are and were. The verb from {verb:...} takes the plural form, as in 'they play'. Every helper still gives a word, so no braces are left and the sentence still reads as a normal they/them sentence. This happens when the pronoun service has none for the person, or the person never chatted on Twitch where the bot is, and they never picked pronouns in the bot.
answers.quote: If the bot has no pronouns for a person, it uses they, them, their, person, are and were.

answers.answer: I had to guess with a he/they viewer. The page lists he/they as one of the mixed sets, which gives he, them and their. Later it advises putting he/him as the main set and they/them as the second set, which gives he, him and his. I had to reread to choose between the two. Smaller point: the !lurk getting food example comes after the general rule, and only then did I learn that a bare helper treats any first word as a person.
answers.quote: So for a viewer who uses he/they, put he/him as the main set and they/them as the second set.

answers.answer: The neopronoun and mixed-set paragraphs are long runs of word lists when read aloud. They repeat the same 'person' and 'is and was' reasoning twice, which costs attention on detail most readers will not act on.
answers.quote: Both give “person” as the gendered term, and both take is and was, because only “they” takes the plural verb.

warning_review.reason: Five short sentences, each one rule the reader needs before writing a reply: where pronoun helpers are refused, what bare {tense} does without a person, and what to write in a viewer's own text. These are access and behavior facts that change the steps, and the reader answered question 2 from them without trouble. Splitting or trimming them would not help a reader who is about to edit a reply.

Six short sentences that each settle one part of who a bare helper follows: the first typed word, a leading @ removed, the sender when nothing follows, and the two examples (!hug @someone, !lurk getting food). The reader needs this to avoid a wrong person in a reply, and the examples show the surprise directly. No sentence is filler, so the length is not a defect.
